name: Revigator radon water crock

card.summary: The Revigator was a 1920s ceramic crock with a radioactive lining that irradiated overnight water, marketed as a health tonic.
card.note: Historical product; later analysis found radon plus arsenic, lead and uranium in the water.

quick.overview:
The Revigator was a ceramic water crock lined with radioactive ore. Users filled it at night and drank the irradiated water the next day. It was sold as a health tonic and belongs to the early-twentieth-century fashion for radioactive products, some of which were marketed for beauty and vitality.

It was promoted against arthritis, flatulence and senility. A Mount St. Mary's University study cited on Wikipedia concluded that the radiation risk was probably low compared with other causes of death at the time, though water from vintage units also contained arsenic, lead, vanadium and uranium.
quick.how: Historically, users filled the crock every night and drank freely from it. It is no longer sold as a health product; vintage crocks are collectors' items.
quick.risks: Analysis of water stored in a vintage Revigator found high radon along with arsenic, lead, vanadium and uranium at levels that pose health risks.

lead: The Revigator was a ceramic water crock with a radioactive lining. Water left in it overnight was drunk the next day, and the product was promoted as promoting health and vitality, which in era marketing included a youthful look.[1]

R. W. Thomas patented the device in 1912 and began manufacturing in southern California by 1923. In 1924 he sold the business to Dow-Herriman Pump & Machinery, which sold thousands of units during the 1920s and 1930s.[1] The lining contained carnotite and the crock had a lead spout.[1]

Claims included prevention of arthritis, flatulence and senility.[1] Radon spa therapy has since been studied separately in controlled settings, but those studies concern bathing and are not tests of the Revigator.

chain: Water sits in radioactive crock overnight
angle.text: Buyers drank the water hoping for vitality and relief from ailments, in the era's wider radium-for-beauty fashion.

paras: Thomas patented it in 1912, moved production to California by 1923, and sold the business in 1924 to Dow-Herriman.[1] Instructions told users to fill the jar every night and drink freely.[1]

Analysis of overnight water from a vintage unit found high radon levels, plus arsenic, lead, vanadium and uranium at levels that pose health risks. A Mount St. Mary's University study concluded the radiation risk was probably low relative to other causes of death at the time.[1]
No studies found for the Revigator itself. Separate research covers radon spa baths, for example a randomised trial of radon baths in osteochondrosis rehabilitation.[2]

timeline.event: R. W. Thomas patents the device.[1]
